subject: Business
title: Opportunity Cost: The Road Not Taken
description: A 60-second lesson on Opportunity Cost: The Road Not Taken.

hook.text: You buy a $1,200 phone. The real cost isn't $1,200 — it's the $1,200 investment that would've grown to $5,000 in 15 years.

buildup.text: Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative you give up when making a choice.

discovery.text: Every dollar spent is also a dollar not invested, not saved, and not used for something else.

twist.text: Free things have opportunity costs too. Time spent scrolling social media is time not spent learning or earning.

climax.text: Jeff Bezos used opportunity cost to leave a Wall Street job: the regret of not trying Amazon outweighed the risk.

punchline.text: Every 'yes' is a hidden 'no' to something else.

quiz.question: What is opportunity cost?
options: The value of the next best alternative you give up
The price printed on a product label
A tax charged on investment returns

details.summary: Opportunity cost is the value of the best alternative you give up when making a choice. Every financial decision has an opportunity cost because money, time, and resources spent one way cannot simultaneously be used for something else.
details.whyItMatters: Thinking in terms of opportunity cost transforms financial decisions. A 50,000 dollar car is not just 50,000 dollars but also the investment returns that money could have generated over decades of compounding growth.
takeaways: Every choice has a hidden cost: the best alternative you forgo
Financial opportunity cost includes forgone investment returns over time
Evaluating opportunity costs leads to more intentional spending decisions

faq.question: How do you calculate the opportunity cost of a purchase?
faq.answer: Consider what the money could earn if invested instead. A 30,000 dollar purchase invested at 8 percent for 30 years would grow to about 300,000 dollars. The true opportunity cost of the purchase is the future wealth you forgo, not just the sticker price.

faq.question: Does opportunity cost only apply to money?
faq.answer: No. Time has opportunity cost too. Spending two hours commuting daily represents thousands of hours over a career that could have been used for exercise, education, family, or side work. The best decision-makers weigh both financial and time-based opportunity costs.
